nameStory: The Silver-sided Sector Spider gets its name from two distinctive features that make it easy to spot. The 'silver-sided' part comes from the shimmery, leaf-like markings on the female's abdomen that catch the light like polished metal. The 'sector' refers to its famous web design quirk – it deliberately leaves out a slice of its circular web, like a pie with a missing piece.
description: This small orb weaver spider is best known for its unusual web-building habits and distinctive markings. Female Silver-sided Sector Spiders sport a yellowish-brown front section and a striking leaf-shaped silver marking on their rounded abdomen. These solitary spiders are master architects, spinning fresh orb webs daily with their signature missing sector. They're part of the orb weaver family, those classic spiders that create the circular webs we often walk into on dewy mornings.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for circular orb webs with a distinctive missing wedge-shaped section, like a pie slice was cut out – this gap is always consistent and intentional

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Females have a silvery, leaf-shaped marking on the back of their rounded abdomen that shimmers in sunlight, contrasting with their yellow-brown front section

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Spider sits in a retreat connected to the web by a signal line, feeling for vibrations when prey gets caught in the sticky spiral threads

idTips.label: Web Location
idTips.description: Webs are typically built near human structures – window frames, porch corners, and building edges where flying insects are common

habitat: Silver-sided Sector Spiders prefer areas around human habitation in New England, particularly favoring building exteriors, window frames, and porch corners. They thrive in suburban and urban environments where artificial lighting attracts flying insects. Look for their distinctive webs on structures rather than in wild forest settings.

seasonality.spring: Juvenile spiders emerge in late spring and begin building their first webs, though these are smaller and less distinctive than adult webs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, with females displaying their full silver markings and males actively searching for mates before dying after reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Females produce egg sacs in late autumn and may be seen guarding them, while their webs become less frequently rebuilt as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive winter; the species overwinters as eggs or early juveniles in protected locations.

funFact: These spiders intentionally build their webs with a missing sector and run a 'telephone line' from their hiding spot directly to the web's center – when prey hits the web, vibrations travel instantly down this signal thread, alerting the spider to dinner without having to watch the web constantly.
confusionNotes: The missing sector web is so distinctive that confusion with other orb weavers is rare – most other circular web builders complete their full spiral pattern. If you see a 'broken' orb web, check if the gap is consistent and intentional rather than accidental damage.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an orb weaver, this spider was recently reclassified from the traditional orb weaver family (Araneidae) to a smaller family called Phonognathidae, though many field guides still list it under the old classification. This taxonomic shuffle doesn't change how you identify it in the field.
compareHints: The Silver-sided Sector Spider differs from its relative the Red-sided Sector Spider primarily in coloration – where this species has silvery leaf-like markings, the Red-sided has reddish markings on its abdomen. Both species create the characteristic missing-sector webs, but the Silver-sided is more commonly found around human structures while Red-sided species prefer more natural settings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative the Silver-sided Sector Spider, the Red-sided species is more brownish in color and strictly avoids human habitation, preferring wild rocky and bushy areas.
